tabs.title: Understanding the text
tabs.description: Read for meaning and significant details.

tabs.title: Real-life decisions
tabs.description: Apply a useful idea in a new setting.

questions.q: Why does the engineer ask students to investigate before putting up a sign by the stream?
choices: She thinks only adults should discuss litter problems.
The school has already paid for too many signs.
She wants them to stop cleaning the river.
The place where rubbish is found may not be where it begins its journey.
questions.explanation: The engineer redirects attention from litter at the stream to how it enters drains upstream.

questions.q: What does the street drain help the students understand?
choices: The bus stop produces no rubbish at all.
Rain can carry street litter through pipes towards the stream.
All street drains carry water to the sea.
Rubbish cannot travel far once it enters a pipe.
questions.explanation: The explanation connects light rubbish on pavements to rainfall and drainage pipes.

questions.q: Why is the difference between the bus stop and the library significant?
choices: It helps identify where most litter is likely to enter the drainage system.
It means the library is responsible for every wrapper.
It proves that people never litter near libraries.
It shows that rain always falls harder at bus stops.
questions.explanation: The large difference in counts points to a local concentration of rubbish by the busy stop.

questions.q: What does the conversation with the bus driver add to the students' findings?
choices: A reason to move the bus stop away from the town.
Proof that the café never serves snacks to bus passengers.
A practical explanation for why the bin fills before the busiest time.
Evidence that bus drivers are responsible for all the rubbish.
questions.explanation: The driver explains that the bin is emptied early and fills by the afternoon.

questions.q: Why do students count wrappers after the last lesson?
choices: They need to finish before the engineer comes.
They are only allowed to work outside the school at night.
They expect to find fewer visitors at that time.
They want to observe the street when the bus stop is busy.
questions.explanation: The group records litter when bus-stop use is high, to understand the pattern.

questions.q: Why do both the café and the council change something?
choices: The problem involves both customer behaviour and waste-bin management.
The engineer learns that the stream is already clean.
The council decides the café must close.
The children refuse to continue the investigation.
questions.explanation: The practical response addresses the café's surroundings and the timing/location of the bin.

questions.q: Why do students avoid claiming that their project solved the problem completely?
choices: They had not spoken to anybody who used the street.
Wind and future storms could reveal other sources of litter.
The stream remained full of wrappers after every rainfall.
Their findings showed no clear pattern at all.
questions.explanation: The article notes other roads and new weak points could continue to contribute rubbish.

questions.q: Residents begin sending photos of litter from other streets. Why is this useful?
choices: It means the students no longer need to check the data.
It lets the town ignore future rainstorms.
It helps identify additional locations that the first survey might have missed.
It proves the council is responsible for every piece of rubbish.
questions.explanation: The community observations extend the evidence beyond the original bus-stop area.

questions.q: A school finds rubbish downstream after heavy rain. What should it investigate next?
choices: Whether the school can stop all rainfall.
The colours of litter seen in the water.
Only the number of signs beside the water.
Where street rubbish enters drains before reaching the stream.
questions.explanation: The engineer's advice is to trace the pathway of litter rather than focus only on where it appears.

questions.q: Which question best reflects the students' change in thinking?
choices: Who should put more signs beside the stream?
Where does the rubbish start, and which conditions allow it to travel?
Which group of people should we blame first?
How can we hide the litter from visitors?
questions.explanation: The final question shifts from visible litter to sources and causes.
